items.title: James Moody — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: And then we went on tour with Ella Fitzgerald, you know, it was like Ella Fitzgerald with the Dizzy Gillespie Orchestra.

ctx.x: Now, in The Spotlight, did you all stay in The Spotlight all that time, or were you working all sorts of places across that couple of years you were?

No, we were there for weeks. We played for a week, maybe two weeks, and then -­ and then we would go somewhere else, like we'd do the Apollo Theater. Like, they had a chitling [phonetic sp.] circuit that we did, you know, and we'd go the Apollo Theater in New York, and then we'd go the Howard Theater -- no -- the Apollo Theater in New York then you go to the Royal Theater [phonetic sp.] in Baltimore, then you go to the Howard Theater in Washington, and then you go down South and go to some of these little…
So you all were real aware -- you were very aware of the activities of the Klan and other groups in all the areas that you were traveling through?

items.title: James Moody interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998
items.q: I was on the bus when we were doing a tour with Ella Fitzgerald

ctx.x: That’s distressing to hear. In fact, Ruth Brown told us a story about how she got pulled over and all the musicians were in the car and they had to get out and play on the side of the road to prove — because they had a Cadillac or something.

Well I was on the bus when we were doing a tour with Ella Fitzgerald and we were late for the gig, about two hours late, and we pulled up to the place, like I mean everybody had gone and all like that. And the guy pointed to Ella Fitzgerald, she had her hair all wrapped up in her thing, and she wasn’t feeling well, tired, and the owner of the place wanted her to sing for his wife. I mean we finally got out of it, but I mean he wanted her to sing. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
Did things get better in the 60s with the Civil Rights movement and all that? Did it get better?
